issues.legal_issue: A statutory presumption of corrupt receipt is not rebutted by a plausible alternative explanation unless the explanation is supported by evidence.
material_facts: The accused, a public official, accepted money from the complainant after asking whether the complainant had brought it; the complainant and an accompanying witness testified to the demand and payment, and the money was recovered from the accused.

The accused claimed that he had received the money as repayment of a government loan, but the evidence showed that no amount was due from the complainant and that the recovery instruction concerned a debt owed by the complainant’s brother.

The asserted demand notice was not shown to have been sent by registered post or delivered personally, and the certificate of posting was obtained from a different location and was unsupported by a maintained postal record.
issues.conclusion: The explanation that the money was received as repayment of government dues was unsupported and did not rebut the statutory presumption; the evidence established receipt as illegal gratification.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 4 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, proof that an accused accepted gratification other than legal remuneration attracts a presumption that it was accepted as a motive or reward of the kind referred to in Section 161 IPC. The accused need not prove the defence beyond reasonable doubt, but must establish it on the basis of evidence, directly or by legally available inference; a bare or merely plausible explanation under Section 313 CrPC is insufficient. Dhanvantrai Balvantrai Desai v. State of Maharashtra explains that the contrary must be proved, while Chaturdas Bhagwandas Patel v. State of Gujarat states that the defence must establish with reasonable probability that the money was accepted for another reason. Punjabrao v. State of Maharashtra was distinguished because there the debt and the accused’s loan-collection activity on the day of payment were undisputed. A certificate of posting, without a maintained dispatch record, may provide very little assistance when dispatch is disputed.

rule.if: presumption_applicable_corruption_case and public_official_received_nonlegal_gratification and lawful_payment_explanation_offered and not explanation_supported_by_evidence

predicates.presumption_applicable_corruption_case: The proceeding concerns an offence for which the law presumes that accepted non-legal gratification was received as a corrupt motive or reward.
predicates.public_official_received_nonlegal_gratif: A public official accepted money that was not shown to be legal remuneration.
predicates.lawful_payment_explanation_offered: The accused claimed that the money was received for a lawful purpose other than as corrupt gratification.
predicates.explanation_supported_by_evidence: Evidence in the record supports the accused’s account of the lawful purpose for which the money was received.

issues.definition: When a public official accepts non-legal gratification in a proceeding covered by the presumption, an offered lawful-payment account that lacks evidentiary support leaves the presumption unrebutted.

issues.legal_issue: An acquittal must be set aside in a State appeal when the evidence permits only the conclusion that the accused is guilty.
material_facts: The State appealed from an acquittal entered by the High Court after the trial court had convicted the accused.
The complainant’s account of demand, payment and acceptance was corroborated by an accompanying witness, and the money was recovered from the accused.
The High Court accepted an explanation that lacked support in the evidence and did not account for the evidence of demand, payment and acceptance.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in acquitting the accused; the acquittal was set aside and the trial court’s conviction was restored.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal against acquittal, the appellate court will not interfere where two views are possible and the acquittal view is not wholly improbable. Where the record leads only to the conclusion of guilt, the acquittal cannot stand. The Court relied on State of Andhra Pradesh v. K. Narasimhachary (2005).

rule.if: state_appeal_from_acquittal and prosecution_evidence_corroborates_demand_and_acceptance and defense_explanation_lacks_record_support and record_permits_only_guilt_conclusion

predicates.state_appeal_from_acquittal: The State appealed a judgment acquitting an accused after a trial court conviction.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_corroborates_demand: The prosecution evidence corroborates that the accused demanded and accepted the payment.
predicates.defense_explanation_lacks_record_support: The accused’s alternative explanation for receiving the payment is unsupported by the evidence in the record.
predicates.record_permits_only_guilt_conclusion: On the evidence as a whole, guilt is the only reasonable conclusion and the acquittal view is not reasonably available.

issues.definition: In a State appeal from an acquittal, corroborated evidence of demand and acceptance combined with an unsupported defence and a record permitting only guilt requires the acquittal to be set aside.

issues.legal_issue: A sentence may be reduced in light of prolonged proceedings and the offender’s personal circumstances while the conviction is restored.
material_facts: The Court restored convictions for offences under Section 161 IPC and Section 5(2) read with Section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947.
The matter had remained pending through the trial, the High Court appeal and the appeal before the Supreme Court for a prolonged period.
The offender had been relatively young when the incident occurred, came from a poor background and had a family to support.
issues.conclusion: The Court maintained the convictions but reduced the custodial sentences, directing that they run concurrently.
issues.legal_principle: The Court exercised its sentencing discretion in view of the long passage of time and the offender’s age, background and family responsibilities. No earlier case was cited for this sentencing determination.

rule.if: conviction_restored_on_appeal and proceedings_were_protracted and offender_was_young_at_offense and offender_had_poor_background_and_family_responsibilities

predicates.conviction_restored_on_appeal: The appellate court restored the offender’s conviction after overturning an acquittal.
predicates.proceedings_were_protracted: The criminal proceedings remained pending for a prolonged period across the trial and appeals.
predicates.offender_was_young_at_offense: The offender was relatively young when the offence occurred.
predicates.offender_had_poor_background_and_family_: The offender came from a poor background and had a family to support.

issues.definition: When a conviction is restored after prolonged proceedings and the offender was young at the offence and has a poor background and family responsibilities, the sentence is reduced.
